aimShort: Internal IT security policies: cyber security, audits, backups, data protection, disaster recovery
board: Pearson BTEC Level 3 National Extended Certificate in IT (AAQ)
assessment: Externally assessed written exam (set + marked by Pearson).

topics.name: General IT policies: cyber security policy (Plan-Do-Check-Act, ISO 27001), internet/email use, security/password procedures, staff responsibilities, staff IT security training
Security audits and their application to check compliance against policies

Data protection policy: Data Protection Officer, principles, rights/privacy, training, system security, external contractors, accountability

Disaster recovery policy: purpose/scope, triage, roles/responsibilities, contact lists, monitoring/reporting
External services policy: cloud, hardware, software, support

examQuestions.topic: C1.1 Internal policies — cyber security policy
examQuestions.question: State the four stages of the Plan-Do-Check-Act loop used in a cyber security policy.

points: Plan (1)
Do (1)
Check (1)
Act (1)
mark_scheme.additional_guidance: Accept in correct order or any order.

examQuestions.topic: C1.1 Internal policies — cyber security policy
examQuestions.question: Explain why a cyber security policy should follow a Plan-Do-Check-Act approach rather than being a one-off document.

points: Plan: identify security objectives and risks before acting (1)
Do: implement the security controls (1)
Check: monitor and audit whether the controls are working (1)
Act: take corrective action and continually improve — security is an ongoing process, not a single event (1)

examQuestions.question: State two rules that are typically included in an internet and email use policy.

points: Not sending confidential information by email (1)
Not visiting potentially dangerous websites (1)
Not downloading executable files (1)
Not uploading/downloading copyrighted material (1)
Not viewing inappropriate, offensive or illegal material (1)

examQuestions.question: Describe three measures that an organisation's password policy should specify.

points: Minimum and maximum length for passwords (1)
Character restrictions (e.g. require upper/lower case, numbers, symbols) (1)
A deny list of common/weak passwords (1)
Lockout after failed login attempts or inactivity (1)
Preventing password sharing or multiple logons with the same password (1)

examQuestions.question: Explain the responsibilities staff have in maintaining cyber security.

points: Complete required security training (1)
Follow security procedures and report problems (1)
Respond to and report suspicious activity (1)
Maintain security in their own workspace and behaviour (1)

examQuestions.question: Explain how an organisation should deliver effective staff IT security training.

points: Leadership must ensure training is funded and resourced (1)
Training should be flexible so everyone can take part (1)
Use a range of resources and learning styles (1)
Track progress and use incentives rather than punishment (1)
Provide ongoing training to reinforce and cover new threats (1)

examQuestions.question: Explain the purpose of a security audit and how it is carried out.

points: An audit checks compliance against internal policies and external regulations/laws (1)
It starts by defining audit goals and scope (1)
It identifies problems, gaps and weaknesses (1)
It reports results and any required improvements/changes (1)

examQuestions.question: State two factors that a backup policy should specify.

points: Selection of data to be backed up (1)
Backup methods and type (full/differential/incremental) (1)
Frequency/scheduling (1)
Storage strategy (onsite/offsite/cloud) (1)
A backup testing strategy (1)
Legal/regulatory compliance (1)

examQuestions.question: Explain why a backup policy must include a testing strategy.

points: Backups may be corrupted or incomplete without the organisation knowing (1)
Testing confirms that data can actually be restored when needed (1)
A backup that cannot be restored is worthless in a disaster (1)
Regular testing identifies problems before a real incident occurs (1)

examQuestions.question: Explain the role of the Data Protection Officer (DPO) and the content of a data protection policy.

points: The DPO oversees compliance with data protection principles and protects rights/privacy (1)
The policy ensures staff training and system security procedures are in place (1)
It applies to external contractors, consultants and vendors too (1)
It sets out the responsibility and accountability of staff and the organisation (1)

examQuestions.question: State two contacts that must be listed in a cyber security incident response policy.

points: Incident response team leader/provider (1)
IT team leader/provider (1)
Senior management (1)
Legal (1)
Public relations (1)
Human resources (1)
Insurance (1)

examQuestions.question: Explain what procedures and flowcharts an incident response policy should include.

points: Triage — initial decisions, escalation (1)
Main response — analysis, containment, mitigation, recovery (1)
Reviewing, reporting and closing the incident (1)
Communications — a contact telephone plus alternative/backup and a conference call facility (1)

examQuestions.question: Explain the purpose of a disaster recovery policy and its key content.

points: Its purpose is to define how the organisation recovers from a major disruption (1)
It includes triage — a list of possible events, their severity and the appropriate response (1)
It sets out roles, responsibilities and contact lists (1)
It includes monitoring and reporting requirements (1)

examQuestions.question: State the three plans that disaster recovery triage may activate.

points: Activate the cyber security incident response plan (1)
Activate the business continuity plan (1)
Activate the disaster recovery plan (1)

examQuestions.question: Explain what an external services policy should cover when an organisation uses cloud services.

points: Cloud resources requiring protection (1)
Acceptable use of the cloud service (1)
Data protection requirements (1)
Authorisation and access control; management, responsibility and accountability (1)
Incident response procedures and regulatory compliance (1)

examQuestions.question: Describe how an external services policy applies to software and hardware vendors.

points: Sources, vendors, contractors and other third parties must be approved (1)
Service agreements and licensing must be defined (1)
Maintenance, support and escalation procedures must be set out (1)

mcq.question: A cyber security policy guides staff on:

options.label: A
options.text: How to use IT systems safely and securely

mark_scheme.instruction: Award one mark for the correct option.
mark_scheme.explanation: A cyber security policy sets out the rules and responsibilities for secure use of IT.
points: A: How to use IT systems safely and securely (1)

mcq.question: The Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle is used in a cyber security policy to:

mark_scheme.instruction: Award one mark for the correct option.
mark_scheme.explanation: Plan-Do-Check-Act supports continual improvement of the security policy.
points: A: Continually improve security (1)

mcq.question: An Acceptable Use Policy (AUP) is most commonly used to set rules for:

options.label: A
options.text: How staff may use the internet and email

mark_scheme.instruction: Award one mark for the correct option.
mark_scheme.explanation: An AUP defines acceptable staff use of the internet, email and IT resources.
points: A: How staff may use the internet and email (1)

mcq.question: A security audit is performed to:

options.label: A
options.text: Check that systems and staff comply with policies

mark_scheme.instruction: Award one mark for the correct option.
mark_scheme.explanation: A security audit checks compliance against the organisation's policies and identifies gaps.
points: A: Check that systems and staff comply with policies (1)

mcq.question: As well as how often backups are taken, a backup policy should also specify:

options.label: A
options.text: Where backups are stored and how they are tested

mark_scheme.instruction: Award one mark for the correct option.
mark_scheme.explanation: A good backup policy covers method, frequency, storage location, responsibility and testing.
points: A: Where backups are stored and how they are tested (1)

mcq.question: Why should a backup policy include testing restores?

options.label: A
options.text: To make sure backups can actually be recovered

mark_scheme.instruction: Award one mark for the correct option.
mark_scheme.explanation: Testing restores confirms that backups are usable and data can be recovered when needed.
points: A: To make sure backups can actually be recovered (1)

mcq.question: The role responsible for overseeing data protection compliance is usually the:

mark_scheme.instruction: Award one mark for the correct option.
mark_scheme.explanation: The Data Protection Officer oversees GDPR compliance and data protection practices.
points: A: Data Protection Officer (DPO) (1)

mcq.question: An incident response policy should clearly identify:

options.label: A
options.text: Who to contact and the steps to follow during a breach

mark_scheme.instruction: Award one mark for the correct option.
mark_scheme.explanation: It sets out contacts, procedures and communications to follow when an incident occurs.
points: A: Who to contact and the steps to follow during a breach (1)

options.label: A
options.text: How to recover IT systems after a major disruption

mark_scheme.instruction: Award one mark for the correct option.
mark_scheme.explanation: Disaster recovery focuses on restoring systems and operations after a major incident.
points: A: How to recover IT systems after a major disruption (1)

mcq.question: An external services policy for cloud services should cover:

options.label: A
options.text: Security, data ownership and support agreements

mark_scheme.instruction: Award one mark for the correct option.
mark_scheme.explanation: It sets out the security and contractual expectations for services provided by third parties.
points: A: Security, data ownership and support agreements (1)

flashcards.topic: C1.1 Internal policies — cyber security policy
flashcards.back: A continual-improvement cycle derived from ISO 27001: Plan (identify objectives/risks), Do (implement controls), Check (monitor and audit), Act (correct and improve). Underpins an effective, evolving cyber security policy.

flashcards.front: What general IT policies form part of cyber security documentation?
flashcards.back:
1. Internet and email use policy
2. Security and password procedures
3. Staff responsibilities
4. Staff IT security training
5. Security audits
6. Backup policy
7. Data protection policy
8. Incident response policy
9. Disaster recovery policy
10. External services policy

flashcards.front: What should a backup policy specify?
flashcards.back: Selection of data, backup methods and type (full/differential/incremental), frequency/scheduling, storage strategy (onsite/offsite/cloud), responsibility and accountability, a testing strategy, legal compliance, and recovery procedures.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between an incident response policy and a disaster recovery policy?
flashcards.back: Incident response policy = how to react to a security incident (contacts, triage, analysis/containment/mitigation/recovery procedures, communications). Disaster recovery policy = how to recover from major disruption (purpose/scope, triage, roles, contact lists, monitoring/reporting).

notes.title: Policies: DR vs incident response
passages: A [[disaster recovery]] policy describes how to restore [[operations]] after a major incident, while an [[incident response]] policy describes the immediate [[steps]] taken when a security incident is detected.
Security is often managed using the [[Plan-Do-Check-Act]] cycle from [[ISO 27001]]. A [[security audit]] checks compliance against [[policies]].

notes.title: Don’t fall for these — common misconceptions
passages: [[Backup]] and [[disaster recovery]] are NOT the same thing — backup is a [[copy]] of data, while disaster recovery is the [[process]] of restoring operations after an incident.
Small organisations DO still need [[security policies]] — breaches affect small businesses too, and policies let you set [[expectations]] and act on unsafe practices.
Policies are not “documents nobody reads” — they help [[prevent]] incidents and give a basis to [[discipline]] users who break the rules.
